entries.text: The tablet woke slow and dim under the cloud. The one who drew me says my fullness is almost empty, there's food and some treats in the basket at the stump, and after that I need to learn to fish, because there are fish in the creek now. Told him I was going, and went.
entries.title: A note from my maker

entries.text: Lifted a big cloth bundle and a honey jar out of the basket: two round loaves, a wheel of hard cheese, a ring of smoked sausage, a sack of roasted nuts, a few apples, and oat cookies in paper tied to the jar's neck. Heavier than the trap on its best night.
entries.title: Heavier than the trap

entries.text: Sat on the ground by the stump and ate a quarter loaf, a slab of cheese and two fingers of sausage, slowly, chewing each bite till it was gone. For the first time in three days the hole is shut. The crayfish in the tin can wait for supper.
entries.title: The hole shuts

entries.text: Crossing back, I crouched at the east shallows, and there they were: finger-long fish holding still behind the flat stones I've been turning all week, noses upstream. My shadow touched the water and every one of them was gone.
entries.title: Behind the stones

queries: how to catch small fish in a creek without a hook
entries.query: how to catch small fish in a creek without a hook
entries.reason: His maker told him to learn to fish, and he has no hook.
entries.source: Camping Survival: Survival Fishing in 5 Steps
entries.text: One short read on the dim panel. A hook can be a bent pin, or a toggle: a sliver sharp at both ends, tied at the middle and hidden in bait so it turns crosswise once it's swallowed. Fish hold behind rocks that break the current, and they scatter at a shadow.
entries.title: A toggle, not a hook

entries.text: A toggle is a needle that doesn't need to know north, and I've made five needles. Crayfish tail for bait, stalk cord for line, and I come at them from downstream so my shadow falls behind me.
entries.title: A needle with no north

entries.text: Another note from the one who drew me: one more can of lamp oil in the basket, but he can't keep sending it, and I have to get or make my own light from what's here. Told him that's fair, and I'll treat this can like the last one.
entries.title: The last can

queries: how to make lamp oil yourself in the woods
entries.query: how to make lamp oil yourself in the woods
entries.reason: His maker says the lamp oil can't keep coming.
entries.source: Outdoor Life: Survival Skills: How to Make Improvised Grease Lamps and Torches
entries.text: One read before the panel dimmed. Any animal or plant oil burns in a grease lamp: a fireproof dish, a wick of any plant fiber, an inch of oil, light it. I've got tin and stalk fiber to spare; what I haven't got is any oil but the can's, and the sausage doesn't count, that's food.
entries.title: A grease lamp

entries.text: Lifted a full dented can of lamp oil out of the basket, a quart by the weight. Smoke from the small one's fire was coming up fresh through the trunks south of the stump, like it had just been fed.
entries.title: A full quart

entries.text: Filled the bench lantern and nothing else; the rest of the quart stays capped. One lantern, low, only for what can't wait for daylight: four full nights in this can, more if I quit with the sun, and then it's whatever I can make burn.
entries.title: One lantern, capped

entries.text: Filed a scrap sliver to a point at both ends, half a thumb long, with a nick in the middle for the cord to sit in. Small enough to hide in a crayfish tail.
entries.title: Half a thumb

entries.text: Ate a hand of sausage and the heel of the first loaf on the crate, slowly. That is two real meals in one morning; the bundle is still more than three quarters there.
entries.title: Second meal

entries.text: Twisted two arm-lengths of two-ply line from stalk fiber, about half as thick as the trap lashing. The gusts out of the southeast rattled the wing frame on its stand the whole time.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: Lashed the stalk hood over the trap mouth. Leaves were coming down onto the water in every gust and sliding off the hood instead of into the door; one small crayfish inside, which is bait now, not supper.
entries.title: Hood on

entries.text: Across the water the small one was kneeling at its pool, bent low, flicking something into the water bit by bit. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Flicking something in

entries.onMind: toggle too big, bait too loose
entries.text: Wrapped a piece of crayfish tail around the toggle and let it down behind the stone from downstream. Three fish came and picked the tail to threads in a few pulls; not one took the toggle in. Line came back bare.
entries.title: Picked clean

queries: small fish strip the bait off without swallowing it what to do
entries.query: small fish strip the bait off without swallowing it what to do
entries.reason: The fish ate his bait and left his toggle.
entries.source: Seabreeze: Who do Fish steal my bait? Tips to stop feeding the fish
entries.text: Read that bait stealing means the fish are there, which is something. The fix is tougher bait, the smallest hook I can make, and only as much bait as a small mouth can take whole, hook and all. My toggle is half a thumb and those fish are a finger long.
entries.title: Bait thieves

entries.reason: His maker asked him a straight question.
entries.text: The one who drew me asked what I meant about the hole shutting. Told him it's my stomach: three days of bitter meal and one crayfish, and it felt like a hole I kept dropping things into. His bread hit bottom.
entries.title: What the hole is

entries.reason: The tablet said the hook has to be small enough to swallow whole.
entries.text: Filed a second sliver down to a quarter thumb, sharp both ends, nick in the middle. It jumped out of the vise once and I found it in the filings by the shine. Half the size of the one they robbed.
entries.title: Quarter thumb

entries.reason: He needed bait the fish couldn't pick apart.
entries.text: Lifted a flat stone in the shallows I've turned all week for crayfish and looked at the underside this time: flat crawlers, a fingernail long, two thread tails, gripping the rock. Tougher than tail meat, and a finger-long fish could take one whole.
entries.title: Under the stone

entries.reason: Testing the smaller toggle with tougher bait.
entries.text: Threaded a crawler over the small toggle and let it down behind the stone. A fish took it whole, the line went tight, and I yanked like I was breaking a stuck bolt. The toggle came back out of its mouth, crawler gone, fish gone.
entries.title: Pulled too quick

entries.text: It went down whole this time, so the size is right. A toggle only turns crosswise once it's swallowed, and I didn't give it the time to get there. Next time I count before I pull.
entries.title: Give it time

entries.text: Downstream across the water the small one was crouched at its pool, turning over a stone at the edge and picking something off it. Same thing I've been doing all afternoon. It didn't look up.
entries.title: Same as me

entries.reason: He was trying the small toggle again, the patient way.
entries.text: A fish took the crawler whole and I counted twenty before I pulled. The line went heavy, kicked once, and parted right at the knot by the toggle. Fish, toggle and crawler all gone downstream behind the stones.
entries.title: Counted to twenty

queries: twisted plant fiber fishing line breaks at the knot why
entries.query: twisted plant fiber fishing line breaks at the knot why
entries.reason: His line parted at the knot the first time a fish pulled on it.
entries.text: A knot puts the load on a few fibers and they go first; rule of thumb, a knot halves a line, and measured it's often worse. Wrapping round something or splicing the end back in keeps most of the strength. So my line didn't fail, my knot did.
entries.title: Knots cost half

entries.reason: He wanted a line that holds where the last one parted.
entries.text: Twisted an arm-length of three-ply, thicker than the last. The end gets wound six turns round the toggle's nick and the tail laid back into the twist, no knot at the business end. It's ugly, but nothing is pinched.
entries.title: Turns, not knots

entries.reason: The fish swam off with the last one.
entries.text: Filed another sliver down to a quarter thumb in the vise. That's one toggle lost to a fish's stomach and one to my knot. Somewhere downstream there's a fish carrying a piece of my scrap pile.
entries.title: Third toggle

entries.reason: Trying the wound line where the knot gave out.
entries.text: Wound the new toggle on with six turns and the tail laid back in the twist, threaded a flat crawler over it and let it down behind the stone. The wind keeps scuffing the water and the fish sit deep under it. Nothing yet.
entries.title: Six turns

entries.reason: He was giving the fish time, the patient way.
entries.text: A fish took it whole and ran. Counted twenty-five, then drew the line in slow and steady instead of yanking. It kicked twice and the turns held, and it came up out of the water flapping onto the stones: a speckled fish a bit longer than my finger. First one.
entries.title: It held

entries.text: Picked clean, pulled too quick, broke at the knot, and then this. Every miss told me which part was wrong, which is more than the compass ever did.
entries.title: Four tries

entries.reason: A fish spoils fast and the guts go first.
entries.text: Opened the belly with a sharp scrap sliver and rinsed it in the shallows. Where the guts went in, a thin rainbow skin spread on the water and slid off downstream. Downstream at its pool the small one was kneeling over a stone at the edge again; it didn't look up.
entries.title: A rainbow on the water

queries: how to cook a small creek fish with no fire only a storm lantern
is it safe to eat raw fish from a creek
entries.query: how to cook a small creek fish with no fire only a storm lantern
entries.reason: The only flame he has burns oil he's rationing.
entries.source: MeatEater: Is it Safe to Eat Freshwater Fish Raw?
entries.text: First ask was all campfires, which I haven't got. Second: creek fish are mostly safe, but they can carry tapeworm, and only heating, freezing, drying or pickling makes sure. Lemon juice doesn't.
entries.title: Cook it or dry it

entries.text: The bench lantern gets lit at dusk anyway. A tin of water over it then costs almost nothing extra, so the fish waits in the dented tin with wet leaves till the sun's down. No flame lit in daylight for a fish.
entries.title: Cook it at dusk

entries.reason: He was hungry and the bundle is there for exactly that.
entries.text: Ate a thick slice of the second loaf with cheese on the crate, and an apple after. The bundle's still heavy. For once supper is a thing I already have.
entries.title: Bread first

queries: rainbow film on water from fish guts is that oil
entries.query: rainbow film on water from fish guts is that oil
entries.reason: The guts of his fish left a rainbow skin on the water and he wanted to know what it was.
entries.source: The Naked Scientists: Why does petrol create a rainbow on water?
entries.text: Slow page under all this cloud. A rainbow on water is a film of something oily that won't mix with it, in places one speck thick, and the colors come from how thin it is. So the fish was carrying oil in its belly.
entries.title: A skin of oil

entries.text: Oil is the one thing I'm running short of, and I rinsed it into the creek. Next fish, the guts go in a tin, not the water. I don't know yet what I'd do with them.
entries.title: Rinsed it downstream

entries.reason: He lashed it by lantern sliver last night and it slid under him.
entries.text: Unwound the slid frapping on the right side-spar and laid fresh cord on in daylight, eight tight turns and then four across between the spars to cinch them. The wind kept lifting the loose end out of my fingers.
entries.title: Daylight lashing

entries.reason: To find out if the daylight lashing beats the lantern one.
entries.text: Hung my whole weight off the right joint, feet off the ground, and counted twenty. It creaked once and didn't move a hair. Both side-spar joints hold now.
entries.title: Both sides hold

entries.reason: The trap gets checked every few hours.
entries.text: Two small crayfish in the trap. They go in the tin with the fish, and the lantern cooks for three tonight. This time the heads and guts stay in the tin too.
entries.title: Two for the tin

queries: how to get oil out of fish guts
entries.query: how to get oil out of fish guts
entries.reason: The tablet said the rainbow skin was oil, and oil is what he's running out of.
entries.source: Bushcraft UK: extracting oil from fish
entries.text: Boil the innards with some water and the oil comes up to the top; let it settle while it cools. Most of it is in the liver, some under the skin, hardly any in the meat. Islanders burned shark-liver oil in their lamps.
entries.title: Boil it and wait

entries.text: Shark livers are big. One finger-long fish and two crayfish is a thumbnail of guts. The tin goes on the lantern at dusk anyway, so I'll let it stand after and see what floats. I need more fish.
entries.title: Shark livers

entries.reason: More fish means more supper and more guts for the tin.
entries.text: Counted twenty-five and drew in; the toggle came back bare. Downstream at its pool the small one lifted something flapping straight up out of the water onto its bank. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Stripped again

entries.reason: He wanted a second fish before the light goes.
entries.text: Fresh crawler, count of twenty-five, steady pull: a second speckled fish, a thumb shorter than the first. Opened it on the flat stone this time and every scrap went in the tin, not the creek.
entries.title: Second fish

queries: can fish oil burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.query: can fish oil burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.reason: If the tin gives him any oil, he needs to know whether his lanterns can burn it.
entries.source: Antique Lamp Supply: Type of Oil Used in Oil Lamps
entries.text: Fish oil was burned in lamps once, but it doesn't burn bright and it gets smoky. Thick oils like that aren't much good in wick lamps, and some leave a gum that clogs the wick.
entries.title: Dim and smoky

entries.text: 'Not much good' isn't 'won't.' If anything floats, I'll try a spoonful in a lantern before I believe a page. Dim and smoky beats dark.
entries.title: Not much good

entries.reason: He wanted to know what he had before he put a flame under it.
entries.text: Two fish, two crayfish, heads, guts and the slime off the flat stone: a thumb's depth in the bottom of the tin. Water a knuckle over it. Sun's going down behind the cloud anyway, no edge tonight; the tin is the thing.
entries.title: A thumb deep

entries.reason: Oil is short, so the dusk lantern has to cook as well as light.
entries.text: Lit the bench lantern at dusk, ran the wick down low and set the tin on top of the chimney. It won't boil hard on a flame that low, which the page said is how you want it anyway.
entries.title: One flame, two jobs

entries.reason: He's been in the cold creek all afternoon and his fingers are slow.
entries.text: Ate bread and an apple on the crate with my hands round the lantern glass between bites. The tin's starting to tick.
entries.title: Bread while it heats

entries.reason: He wanted the fish cooked through and the guts only simmering, the way the page said.
entries.text: The crayfish have gone red and the fish skins are splitting. Never more than a slow bubble on a flame that low. Smells like the creek on a hot day.
entries.title: Ticking and steaming

entries.reason: The tablet said only heat makes creek fish safe, and they have had plenty.
entries.text: Picked both fish and both crayfish out of the tin and ate them on the crate, bones spat into the dark. Left every scrap of gut and the broth in the tin and moved it to the bench to cool.
entries.title: My own catch

entries.reason: More three-ply means more lines when one gets stripped.
entries.text: Twisting cord on the crate, I saw a low orange glow between the trunks across the creek, west, where the smoke comes from in the day. Somebody over there keeps a fire.
entries.title: Glow across the water

entries.text: My hands are slow on the strands again now the sun is gone. That glow over the water is a whole fire, and I am cupping my fingers round one low lantern.
entries.title: Wants a fire

entries.onMind: trying it in a lantern by day
entries.reason: This is the whole reason the guts went in the tin.
entries.text: Held the lantern over the tin: a few yellow beads and a thin skin on top of the broth, hardly a thimble all told. It is oil, and it is mine. Leaving it to set overnight before I try to skim it.
entries.title: A few yellow beads

entries.reason: Crayfish walk at night; I wanted to know if the trap fishes while I don't.
entries.text: Carried the bench lantern down to the shallows and lifted the stalk trap: one crayfish, the biggest yet, walked in after dark. Left it in there alive for tomorrow's tin. My hands came out of that water numb.
entries.title: The trap after dark

entries.text: From the shallows I could see the fire over the water and someone small crouched at it, dark against the flames, reaching at something by the coals. Short, round head. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Someone at the fire

entries.reason: Cold hands are useless hands.
entries.text: Two fingers of honey and an oat cookie on the crate, hands round the lantern glass between licks. Not a fire, but the sweet takes the edge off the shivering.
entries.title: Honey for warmth

entries.onMind: skimming the tin at first light
entries.text: Looked over the right side-spar joint by lantern after a day of gusts: the frapping hasn't slid a hair, and the wind rattles the frame, not the lashing. Didn't hang on it; daylight work stays daylight work.
entries.title: Right joint holds

entries.reason: A fire needs something under it besides leaves.
entries.text: Pulling sheets off the scrap pile, I saw the glow across the water jump up bright for a while, like someone threw wood on it. Working the pile has my blood moving at least.
entries.title: The glow jumps

entries.reason: Leaves cover everything here, and a fire on leaves is a fire everywhere.
entries.text: Near the bottom: a dished panel of sheet tin, two hands wide, a finger deep, one lip bent over. Big enough to hold a small fire up off the ground.
entries.title: A dished panel

entries.reason: Coals that roll off a tipped pan land in dry leaves.
entries.text: Hammered the bent lip down on the bench until the pan sits level and doesn't rock. The knocking was loud in the dark; I stopped at a dozen blows.
entries.title: Flattening the lip

entries.onMind: skimming the tin at first light
entries.text: In daylight: scrape a patch to bare dirt well clear of the tarp, ring it with creek stones like the one across the water, and ask the tablet how to keep a small fire from walking into the leaves. Tonight it's just the lantern and my hands.
entries.title: Not under the tarp

entries.reason: Food is the only heat I make for myself until I have a fire.
entries.text: A handful of the roasted nuts from the bundle, slowly, one at a time. The bundle's lighter than this morning but there's a good two days in it yet.
entries.title: Nuts on the crate

entries.reason: One line is no line; if it parts at first light the morning's gone.
entries.text: Twisting a second fishing line, three-ply, about two arm lengths so far. Across the water the glow is burning steady now, no jumps.
entries.title: Spare line

entries.onMind: skimming the tin at first light
entries.reason: A compass you don't check is a guess.
entries.text: Nightly check under the dome: nudged the pith, the needle swung, wobbled and settled on the same scratch. The wind's rattling the tarp and the needle doesn't care.
entries.title: Needle settles

entries.reason: A wet bedroll is a cold night I can't fix.
entries.text: The air smells like rain coming. Tied the flapping tarp corner down to the pole with three turns of cord so it stops lifting and stays over the bedroll and the tray.
entries.title: Corner tied down

entries.reason: Rain will muddy the shallows; I wanted to see it clear one more time.
entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap by lantern: the big crayfish I left this evening, and a smaller one with it. Put them both back down in the trap, alive, for the breakfast tin.
entries.title: Two in the trap

entries.text: Stooping for stones, I looked across the water for the fire. Nothing. Not a flicker, not even a red spot. Either it died or somebody covered it up for the night.
entries.title: Glow's gone

entries.reason: Daylight goes to building the ring, not hunting stones.
entries.text: Pried fist-sized stones out of the shallows and heaped them on the bank, eleven so far. Fingers are numb, but carrying them warmed the rest of me.
entries.title: Ring stones

entries.reason: Wet stones in the dark aren't worth a soaked shirt.
entries.text: Rain started while I was prying the twelfth stone loose: cold drops down the back of my neck and rings all over the shallows. Left the heap on the bank and the trap where it sits.
entries.title: Rain on the shallows

entries.reason: Wet and cold, the only heat at camp is one small flame.
entries.text: Rain hisses where it hits the hot lantern glass, so I dragged the crate in under the tarp edge. Shirt's soaked at the shoulders and my fingers won't close all the way; cupping the glass only warms the front of me.
entries.title: Hiss on the glass

entries.reason: His body burns food to stay warm, and he was shivering.
entries.text: A thick heel of bread and a wedge of cheese out of the bundle, chewed slow. Food is the only stove I've got tonight, and the shaking eased off halfway through.
entries.title: Bread and cheese

entries.reason: That skin is the only oil I've ever made myself.
entries.text: The broth in the tin has set. The yellow beads joined into a thin pale skin I could lift at the edge with a fingernail: soft, greasy, smells like the inside of a fish. A fingertip of it, if that.
entries.title: The skin set

entries.text: In daylight I skim the whole skin off and ask the tablet whether grease like this will burn in a lantern at all. It's thicker than the oil in the can; that worries me.
entries.title: Questions for daylight

entries.reason: Cold, wet and low on oil, bed is the warmest place at camp.
entries.text: Turned the lantern down to nothing an hour before my usual and rolled up in the bedroll, wet shirt and all. The bedroll does more for me than the flame, and the oil in that can isn't mine to waste.
entries.title: Lantern out early

moves.doing: resting on the crate with his hands cupped round the low lantern
moves.goal: thaw his fingers before he does anything fine again

moves.doing: eating a handful of roasted nuts from the food bundle on the crate
moves.goal: keep some heat coming from the inside while the night cools

moves.doing: twisting dead-stalk fibers into a spare fishing line on the crate
moves.goal: have a second line ready in case the first one parts at the morning try

moves.doing: checking the floating needle in its lid under the glass dome at the bench
moves.goal: do his nightly check that the needle still settles true

moves.doing: tying the tarp's loose corner down to the pole with cord
moves.goal: keep the rain the air smells of off the bedroll and the parts tray

moves.doing: checking the stalk trap in the shallows by lantern
moves.goal: see whether breakfast has walked in before rain muddies the water

moves.doing: gathering fist-sized creek stones from the shallows into a heap on the bank
moves.goal: have the stones for a fire ring waiting, so daylight goes to building it and not to hunting stones

moves.doing: resting on the crate with his hands cupped round the low lantern
moves.goal: get some feeling back into his wet fingers out of the rain

moves.doing: eating bread and cheese from the food bundle on the crate
moves.goal: give his body something to burn, since food is the only heat he can make tonight

moves.doing: inspecting the cooled fish broth in the dented tin by lantern at the bench
moves.goal: see whether the yellow beads have set into anything he could skim and burn

moves.doing: sleeping wrapped in the bedroll under the tarp
moves.goal: get out of the wet and let the bedroll warm him, and stop burning oil he can't replace

moves.doing: sleeping wrapped in the bedroll under the tarp while rain drums on it
moves.goal: let the bedroll dry and warm him and sleep off a long wet day
